prerequisites: Organisms may contain one cell or many cells.
Distinguish a model diagram from a measured microscopic image.
goals: Explain organisation from organelles to systems.
Identify eight named cell structures and connect each to its role.
Compare typical plant and animal cells while recognising specialisation.
Explain differentiation and evaluate stem-cell benefits and limitations for Paper 2B.
Connect carbohydrates, proteins and lipids to their elements and smaller units.
Design controlled food tests and explain enzyme activity, temperature and pH effects.
Explain diffusion, osmosis and active transport, including concentration and water-potential gradients.
Calculate surface area per volume and evaluate living and non-living transport investigations.
Explain photosynthesis, leaf adaptations and mineral requirements, and evaluate the prescribed plant investigations.
Human nutrition, respiration and later systems and whole-chapter assessment remain unfinished.

sections.title: From organelles to organ systems
paragraphs: An organelle is a specialised structure within a cell, such as a nucleus or mitochondrion. A cell is the basic living unit. A tissue is a group of cells organised to perform a shared function; cells within a tissue need not all be identical.

An organ contains different tissues working together. The stomach includes muscle tissue that moves its contents, glandular tissue that releases substances and other supporting tissues. An organ system consists of organs cooperating in a major process, such as the digestive system.

The sequence is organelle → cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism. These are levels of organisation, not stages through which every object grows. A mitochondrion does not develop into a stomach; cells containing mitochondria are organised into tissues within organs.

The same hierarchy applies to multicellular plants. A leaf contains several tissues, including photosynthetic tissue and transport tissues. Not every organism has every level: a single-celled organism can carry out life processes without organs.

example.question: Place a mitochondrion, a muscle cell, muscle tissue and a heart in increasing organisational order.
steps: Mitochondrion is an organelle.
The muscle cell contains organelles.
Muscle tissue is organised from cells; the heart is an organ containing different tissues.
example.explanation: Classify by what each structure contains and how its parts work together.

practice.question: Why is a heart an organ rather than a tissue?
practice.answer: It contains several tissue types working together in pumping blood.
practice.explanation: Classify by what each structure contains and how its parts work together.

commonMistakes: An organ usually contains several tissue types, not one enormous cell.

sections.title: Five structures shared by typical plant and animal cells
paragraphs: The cell membrane is a thin boundary controlling movement of substances into and out of the cell. It separates the cell contents from its surroundings. A cell wall, when present, lies outside this membrane and has a different role.
Cytoplasm is the material within the cell around its organelles. Many chemical reactions take place there and are catalysed by enzymes. It is not an empty space or a second name for the nucleus.

The nucleus contains most of a eukaryotic cell’s DNA. Genes provide instructions for making proteins, so the nucleus is important in controlling cell activities. It is surrounded by a nuclear envelope and is often represented as a prominent round structure in a schematic.

Mitochondria are organelles in which the later stages of aerobic respiration occur, transferring energy for cellular processes. They have an internal folded membrane; the folds provide a large area for relevant reactions. Plants as well as animals respire and usually have mitochondria.

Ribosomes are small structures where proteins are synthesised. They may appear as dots in an illustrative diagram, but real ribosomes are too small to resolve individually with an ordinary school light microscope. A drawing that uses dots is representing a structure, not showing what every microscope can reveal.

example.question: A cell produces a large amount of protein and has a high energy demand. Name two relevant structures and connect each to its function.
steps: Ribosomes synthesise proteins.
Mitochondria carry out stages of aerobic respiration, transferring energy for cellular activities.
Having the relevant structures supports these activities; their presence alone does not measure the actual rates.
example.explanation: Connect the named structure to the specific process; do not say every organelle simply controls the cell.

practice.question: Do mitochondria release energy only in animal cells?
practice.answer: No. Plant cells also respire and usually contain mitochondria.
practice.explanation: Connect the named structure to the specific process; do not say every organelle simply controls the cell.

commonMistakes: Respiration transfers energy; a mitochondrion does not create energy.
The cell membrane and cell wall are different structures.

sections.title: Cellulose walls, chloroplasts and a permanent vacuole
paragraphs: A plant cell wall is made mainly of cellulose and lies outside the cell membrane. It supports and strengthens the cell. It helps prevent excessive expansion when water enters; it does not replace the selectively permeable membrane.

Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and are the site of photosynthesis. They occur in photosynthetic tissues such as many leaf cells. Root cells growing underground generally have no chloroplasts, so a plant cell need not contain every structure in a typical leaf-cell drawing.

Many mature plant cells have a large permanent vacuole containing cell sap, a solution of substances including sugars and salts. The vacuole is bounded by its own membrane. Water in the vacuole contributes to turgor, helping the cell contents press against the supporting wall.

The wall, vacuole and cytoplasm can be distinguished in a diagram: the wall is the outer supporting boundary, the cell membrane is just inside it, and the vacuole occupies a large internal region in this model. The exact proportions and shapes vary between specialised cells.

example.question: Why is a large vacuole not the same structure as a cell wall?
steps: The vacuole is an internal membrane-bounded region containing cell sap.
The cellulose wall is outside the cell membrane.
Their positions and roles differ, although both contribute to support through turgor.
example.explanation: Give position, contents and function rather than matching two structures because both help support a plant.

practice.question: A root cell has a cellulose wall but no chloroplasts. Is that inconsistent with being a plant cell?
practice.answer: No. Underground roots usually do not photosynthesise and their cells commonly lack chloroplasts.
practice.explanation: Give position, contents and function rather than matching two structures because both help support a plant.

commonMistakes: Do not say every plant cell photosynthesises.
Cell sap is inside the vacuole; it is not the whole cytoplasm.

sections.title: Compare typical cells without turning the model into a rule
paragraphs: Typical plant and animal cells share a nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane, mitochondria and ribosomes. A typical photosynthetic plant cell additionally has a cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts and a large permanent vacuole; the typical animal cell lacks these three features.

These are comparisons of typical models. There are specialised exceptions: mature mammalian red blood cells have no nucleus or mitochondria, and underground root cells normally lack chloroplasts. The animal-cell model also does not imply that animal cells can never contain small membrane-bound vesicles.

Identify cells using structural evidence rather than shape alone. A cell with a cellulose wall is consistent with a plant; a rectangular outline by itself is not proof. If a supplied diagram deliberately omits detail, an unlabelled feature is not automatically absent from the real cell.

In a comparison, state both sides for each feature. “Plant cells have a wall, whereas typical animal cells do not” is clearer than “plants have more structures.” Include similarities when the command asks for similarities and differences.

example.question: A comparison table says plant cells have mitochondria but animal cells do not. Correct it and add one valid difference.
steps: Both typical plant and animal cells contain mitochondria.
Typical plant cells have a cellulose wall; animal cells do not.
A typical photosynthetic plant cell has chloroplasts, but this is not true of every plant cell.
example.explanation: Compare the same named structure on both sides, keeping typical-cell qualifiers.

practice.question: Why is rectangular shape alone a weak identification clue?
practice.answer: Cell shape varies with specialisation and diagrams simplify it. Structural features such as a cellulose wall are more informative.
practice.explanation: Compare the same named structure on both sides, keeping typical-cell qualifiers.

commonMistakes: Absence from a simplified drawing is not always absence from the real cell.

sections.title: Read a labelled cell model and state its limits
paragraphs: The original diagram below is a model of a photosynthetic plant cell beside a typical animal cell. Its symbols locate the eight required structures. It is deliberately simplified and not drawn to a common microscopic scale.

Trace a boundary carefully. The plant’s thick outer boundary represents the wall; the thin boundary inside is the cell membrane. The animal’s single outer boundary represents its membrane. The large internal plant region is its vacuole, while the material surrounding organelles is cytoplasm.

Nuclei, mitochondria and chloroplasts are distinct structures, not different colours of the same organelle. Ribosome dots are enlarged to make them legible. Use the key and structural evidence; do not interpret symbol size as a measured dimension.

For an unfamiliar image or drawing, connect a label to a specific feature and then give its function. Comparing several views and using scale information is stronger than identifying an organelle from colour alone. More real-image interpretation practice is still needed beyond this introductory model.

example.question: A label points to the thick outer boundary of the plant model. Name the structure and distinguish it from the adjacent thin boundary.
steps: The thick outer boundary is the cellulose cell wall.
The thin boundary just inside is the cell membrane.
The wall supports the cell; the membrane controls movement into and out of it.
example.explanation: Identify the exact feature the line reaches, then explain that feature’s role.

practice.question: Does the model prove that ribosomes can be seen with an ordinary light microscope?
practice.answer: No. Its dots are enlarged symbols. Ordinary light microscopy does not resolve individual ribosomes.
practice.explanation: Identify the exact feature the line reaches, then explain that feature’s role.

commonMistakes: Do not use a model’s symbol size as a measured organelle size.

diagram.alt: Original labelled models of a photosynthetic plant cell and a typical animal cell. Both show a nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane, mitochondria and ribosomes. The plant also shows a cellulose wall, chloroplasts and a large vacuole. Symbols are enlarged and not to scale.
diagram.caption: Numbered original models of typical cells; the key identifies eight required structures. The plant model represents a photosynthetic cell, not every plant cell.

sections.title: Differentiation changes what a cell does (Paper 2B)
paragraphs: Differentiation is the development of a cell into a specialised type with structures suited to particular functions. In a developing multicellular organism, many cell types are needed for processes such as absorption, transport, movement and signalling.

Cells with the same genetic information can become different because different genes are active and different proteins are made. That changes their structures and activities. This is a simplified account of gene expression; differentiation is not normally caused by replacing the whole DNA sequence with a new one.

Division and differentiation are different. Division increases cell number; differentiation changes the characteristics and function of a cell. Growth and development may require both, but simply making more identical unspecialised cells does not provide every tissue with the functions it needs.

Some specialised cells have extensive changes, such as the loss of the nucleus during maturation of mammalian red blood cells. This does not make the common explanation that body cells share genetic information useless; it means its scope must be stated carefully. These differentiation requirements apply to Paper 2B.

example.question: Two developing cells begin with the same genetic information. One becomes a muscle cell and another a nerve cell. Explain how different functions can arise.
steps: Different sets of genes are active in the cells.
Different proteins and structures develop.
Those specialisations allow different functions without requiring entirely different starting genomes.
example.explanation: Link gene activity to proteins, cell features and function.

practice.question: Is cell division alone a complete explanation of how specialised tissues develop?
practice.answer: No. Division supplies cells; differentiation gives the cells specialised features and functions.
practice.explanation: Link gene activity to proteins, cell features and function.

commonMistakes: Do not define differentiation as merely increasing the number of cells.

sections.title: Build a structure-to-function explanation (Paper 2B)
paragraphs: A root hair cell has a long extension that increases its surface area for uptake from the soil. Its membrane regulates transport, and respiration supplies energy for active uptake where required. Increasing surface area is different from increasing the whole plant’s height.

A palisade cell in a leaf contains many chloroplasts, helping it absorb light and carry out photosynthesis. A sperm cell has a flagellum for movement, mitochondria associated with the energy demands of movement, and a nucleus carrying genetic information. The named feature must be connected to a relevant function.

A mature mammalian red blood cell has a biconcave form and haemoglobin for oxygen transport. Its form gives a large area relative to volume and a short diffusion distance. It lacks a nucleus, leaving more space for haemoglobin; it does not use mitochondria to power respiration.

These examples illustrate differentiation rather than exhaust every specialised cell in the syllabus. An adaptation answer should follow feature → effect → function. State the direct effect: a long root hair increases exchange area; it does not mean that every dissolved substance enters without control.

example.question: Improve “a root hair cell is long so it is good at absorption.”
steps: Its long extension increases surface area in contact with soil water.
More membrane area is available for uptake.
This supports absorption of water and mineral ions under suitable conditions; specific transport mechanisms still matter.
example.explanation: Give the causal link between a cell feature and its function.

practice.question: Why should a red-cell adaptation answer not say that it contains many mitochondria?
practice.answer: Mature mammalian red blood cells lack mitochondria. Their oxygen transport depends on haemoglobin and their specialised form.
practice.explanation: Give the causal link between a cell feature and its function.

commonMistakes: The presence of an adaptation does not make a cell specialised for every task.

sections.title: Stem cells: potential benefit and specific limitations (Paper 2B)
paragraphs: Stem cells are relatively unspecialised cells that can divide to produce further stem cells and can give rise to specialised cell types. Their differentiation potential varies. Embryonic stem cells can form a wide range of body-cell types; many adult stem cells normally produce a more restricted range.

The potential benefit is replacement of damaged or missing cells with functioning specialised cells. An established example is transplantation of blood-forming stem cells, which can rebuild production of blood cells. This does not mean those cells can automatically replace any tissue in the body.

A proposed cell-replacement treatment must produce the intended cell type, control its growth, deliver it appropriately and achieve a useful function. Cells that divide in a dish are not, by that observation alone, a successful treatment. Uncontrolled growth, contamination and an immune response to donor material can be concerns; their importance depends on the cells and procedure.

Real blood-forming stem-cell transplants can involve substantial risks, including infection and donor cells attacking recipient tissues. The latter is graft-versus-host disease, distinct from the recipient rejecting donor cells. This named transplant example illustrates why an advantage must be weighed against evidence for the particular procedure.

Using embryonic cells can raise ethical objections because obtaining some cell lines involves an embryo. Adult sources may avoid that particular objection but can offer a narrower differentiation range and other practical limitations. Ethical judgements involve values as well as evidence; state the reason for a position instead of treating disagreement as a biological error.

For the syllabus, explain a benefit and a disadvantage, connect each to the specified source or application, and recognise uncertainty. Do not describe every proposed stem-cell use as an available cure or claim that one risk applies equally to every stem-cell procedure. This evaluation requirement is Paper 2B content.

example.question: A report shows that cultured cells divide. A headline claims they will cure every damaged organ. What conclusion is supported?
steps: Division demonstrates growth under the culture conditions.
It does not show the required specialised type, safety, delivery or restored organ function.
Further controlled evidence would be needed; the universal cure claim is unsupported.
example.explanation: Evaluate what the evidence measures and what remains untested.

practice.question: Give one reason adult stem cells can be useful and one reason they may not replace every cell type.
practice.answer: They can supply specialised cells such as blood cells, but many adult stem-cell types have a restricted differentiation potential.
practice.explanation: Evaluate what the evidence measures and what remains untested.

commonMistakes: Do not treat all stem cells as having the same differentiation potential.
A proposed benefit is not proof of a safe, effective treatment.

sections.title: Elements, building units and large molecules
paragraphs: Carbohydrates and the fats and oils considered here contain carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. Proteins contain these elements plus nitrogen; some amino acids also contain sulfur. An element is a type of atom, whereas glucose and an amino acid are molecules. Naming a building unit therefore answers a different question from naming an element.

Starch and glycogen are large carbohydrates built from many glucose units joined together. Plants store carbohydrate as starch; humans store glycogen mainly in liver and muscle cells. Both are polysaccharides. Glucose itself is a small simple sugar, so not every carbohydrate is a large molecule.

Proteins consist of chains of amino acids that fold into specific shapes. Different amino-acid sequences can produce proteins with different structures and functions. Amino acids are the building units, not miniature proteins.

A typical fat or oil molecule, a triglyceride, is formed from one glycerol and three fatty acids. Fats and oils are lipids. Unlike starch or a protein chain, a triglyceride is not a long polymer of one repeating building unit. The specification uses a simple building-unit model; detailed bonding chemistry and the many other kinds of lipid are beyond this introduction.

example.question: A learner writes “Protein contains amino acids, so its extra element is amino acid.” Correct the two ideas.
steps: Protein is built from amino acids; that part identifies its smaller molecular units.
Proteins contain nitrogen as well as carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
An amino acid contains several types of atom and is not itself an element.
example.explanation: Keep the scale of the answer matched to the question: atoms for elements, smaller molecules for building units.

practice.question: Name the smaller units used to build glycogen and a triglyceride.
practice.answer: Glycogen is built from glucose units. A triglyceride is formed from glycerol and three fatty acids.
practice.explanation: The two large molecules use different building units; fatty acids are not sugars.

commonMistakes: Do not list glucose as a chemical element.
Not every carbohydrate is a polysaccharide, and a triglyceride is not a protein-like repeating chain.

sections.title: Testing for reducing sugars and starch
paragraphs: A food test links a reagent and a procedure to an observation. For a solid food, crush a small sample with distilled water. A clear aqueous extract can be used for the reducing-sugar test where needed; for the iodine test, use a separate food portion or slurry so that filtering does not remove the starch being tested. Use separate portions for different tests: one reagent can interfere with another.

For reducing sugars such as glucose, add Benedict's reagent to the aqueous extract and heat in a hot water bath. A positive result is a coloured precipitate, ranging from green or yellow to orange or brick red as the amount of reducing sugar increases under comparable conditions. A negative result remains blue. Benedict's reagent is not specific to glucose: other reducing sugars can also react.

For starch, add iodine solution to a fresh portion of the sample. A blue-black colour is positive; the reagent remains yellow-brown or orange-brown when starch is not detected. Heating is not required. A sample can test positive for both starch and reducing sugar because foods are mixtures.

A distilled-water negative control helps detect contamination; known glucose and starch samples show that their respective tests work. Similar volumes, reagent concentrations and heating times are needed for sensible comparisons. These colour tests alone do not establish an exact concentration. Wear eye protection, use a holder for hot tubes and keep their openings away from people; never taste laboratory food.

example.question: A sample becomes blue-black with iodine and gives an orange precipitate after heating with Benedict's reagent. What does this support?
steps: The iodine result supports the presence of starch.
The Benedict's result supports the presence of a reducing sugar.
It does not identify that sugar uniquely as glucose or give its exact concentration.
example.explanation: State the observation and its specific inference separately.

practice.question: Why is a blue Benedict's result from an unheated mixture not a valid negative test?
practice.answer: The required heating step was omitted, so the test conditions were not met. Repeat the test with a hot water bath and appropriate controls.
practice.explanation: An unchanged colour after an incomplete procedure cannot reliably establish absence.

commonMistakes: Benedict's reagent tests for reducing sugars, not every carbohydrate.
Iodine does not require heating; Benedict's test does.

apparatus: Separate food portions, distilled water, clean tubes, pipettes and eye protection
Benedict’s reagent, iodine and a teacher-controlled hot water bath
method: Crush food with water. Prepare separate portions for the two tests; retain a food portion/slurry for starch.
Add Benedict’s to the sugar-test portion, heat in the water bath and record any coloured precipitate.
Add iodine to the separate starch portion without heating; record whether it becomes blue-black.
variables: Change food sample; record each test observation and inference separately.
Keep sample amount, reagent amount and relevant timing/heating conditions consistent.
safety: Teacher selects samples and reagents; wear eye protection and do not eat laboratory samples.
Use a tube holder and keep hot tube openings away from people.
quality: Run known positive samples and a distilled-water negative control through the same procedure.
Prevent cross-contamination and check starting colour/cloudiness; negative means not detected under these conditions, not proven absolute absence.

sections.title: Testing for protein and lipid
paragraphs: The Biuret test detects peptide bonds in proteins. Add ready-prepared Biuret reagent to an aqueous food extract and mix; a lilac or purple colour is positive, while a negative result remains blue. No heating is required. If separate reagents are used, the sample is first made alkaline with sodium hydroxide, then a few drops of dilute copper sulfate are added. Follow the school protocol rather than adding large amounts of copper sulfate.

For the ethanol emulsion test, mix a fresh food portion with ethanol to dissolve any lipid. Allow insoluble material to settle, then transfer the clear ethanol extract into water. A white, cloudy emulsion supports the presence of lipid because it no longer stays dissolved when the ethanol is diluted. A negative test stays clear. Simply seeing pieces of undissolved food is not a positive emulsion result.

Use a known protein sample and a known oil sample as positive controls, and distilled water as a negative control, each taken through the relevant procedure. Use clean apparatus and separate samples for each test. A food may contain both protein and lipid, and the tests do not measure how nutritious a whole diet is.

Ethanol is highly flammable: use small quantities at room temperature with all flames and ignition sources removed. Do not heat this test. Wear eye protection; alkaline Biuret reagent can damage eyes and skin, and copper-containing waste should follow the teacher's disposal instructions. Do not consume any tested material.

example.question: An ethanol extract is already cloudy before water is added. Why is the student's lipid conclusion uncertain?
steps: Suspended solid food may have caused the existing cloudiness.
The intended observation is a new white emulsion when a clear ethanol extract enters water.
Repeat with a clear extract and compare with positive and negative controls.
example.explanation: The procedure must distinguish the chemical test result from the sample's starting appearance.

practice.question: Which test gives a purple positive result, and should it be heated?
practice.answer: The Biuret test for protein gives a lilac or purple result. It does not need heating.
practice.explanation: The colour change belongs to the protein test; the lipid emulsion is white and cloudy.

commonMistakes: A white emulsion is not the same observation as a purple Biuret result.
Never use a flame near ethanol or combine its test with the Benedict's heating station.

apparatus: Separate food portions, distilled water, clean tubes, pipettes and eye protection
Biuret reagent, ethanol and water; no ignition sources
method: Add ready-prepared Biuret reagent to an aqueous food portion and record any lilac/purple result without heating.
Shake a separate food portion with ethanol away from heat. Let solids settle and transfer clear ethanol extract to water.
Record formation of a new white emulsion; existing suspended solids alone are not a positive result.
variables: Change food sample; record each test observation and inference separately.
Keep sample amount, reagent amount and relevant timing/heating conditions consistent.
safety: Teacher selects samples and reagents; wear eye protection and do not eat laboratory samples.
Ethanol is flammable: remove flames/ignition sources and do not heat this test.
Alkaline Biuret reagent and copper-containing waste require the school handling/disposal protocol.
quality: Run known positive samples and a distilled-water negative control through the same procedure.
Prevent cross-contamination and check starting colour/cloudiness; negative means not detected under these conditions, not proven absolute absence.

sections.title: Enzymes, active sites and metabolic reactions
paragraphs: Metabolism is the collection of chemical reactions in living organisms. Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up these reactions without being used up overall. Enzymes are proteins in the examples studied here, and their folded structure creates an active site.

A substrate binds at an active site with a suitable shape and chemical properties, forming an enzyme–substrate complex. The enzyme helps the reaction proceed with a lower activation energy, and products leave. The enzyme can then catalyse another reaction. Specificity comes from the fit between active site and substrate, rather than from an enzyme choosing what to do.

The simple lock-and-key model represents complementary shapes. Real enzyme molecules can change shape slightly as a substrate binds; a rigid drawing is a model, not a literal description of every movement. A lasting change to the active site may prevent effective substrate binding or catalysis.

Enzymes catalyse both breakdown and synthesis reactions. For example, digestive enzymes break larger food molecules into smaller ones, while other enzymes help build molecules inside cells. An enzyme does not supply energy to the substrate or create energy; it lowers the barrier to a reaction.

example.question: One enzyme molecule converts many substrate molecules during a lesson. Explain how this is possible.
steps: A substrate binds to its active site and is converted into product.
The product leaves, freeing the active site.
The enzyme is not consumed overall and can repeat the catalytic cycle.
example.explanation: Reusability follows from product release and the catalyst remaining available.

practice.question: Why might a protein with an altered active-site shape catalyse its usual reaction much more slowly?
practice.answer: The substrate may no longer bind effectively or be positioned correctly for reaction, so fewer successful catalytic events occur.
practice.explanation: The explanation connects protein structure to function rather than saying that the enzyme has died.

commonMistakes: Enzymes are not living organisms and do not “die”.
A catalyst is not consumed overall, but it can still be damaged or denatured.

sections.title: How temperature and pH change enzyme activity
paragraphs: At low temperature, particles move slowly, so enzyme and substrate collide less often with enough energy for reaction. Warming usually increases reaction rate initially. Above an enzyme's optimum under the test conditions, heat disrupts bonds maintaining its folded shape; the active site changes and the enzyme becomes denatured.

A denatured enzyme usually does not regain its original activity simply by cooling. Ordinary cooling below the optimum usually slows an undamaged enzyme reversibly. Distinguish slower particle movement from loss of the functional active-site structure.

pH affects charges and interactions within the enzyme and at its active site. Each enzyme has a range of pH values over which it works well; moving away from its optimum reduces activity, and sufficiently extreme pH can disrupt its structure. Different enzymes can have different optima, so “all enzymes work best at pH 7” is incorrect.

A rate–temperature graph often rises then drops steeply as denaturation becomes important. A rate–pH graph usually peaks near the optimum and falls on either side. The exact shapes depend on the enzyme and experimental conditions. A peak at one tested temperature identifies the best measured condition, not an exact universal optimum between all possible temperatures.

example.question: An enzyme works slowly at 10 °C, faster at 30 °C, and scarcely at 70 °C. Cooling both the 10 °C and 70 °C samples to 30 °C restores only the first. Explain.
steps: Low temperature reduced particle motion and successful collisions without necessarily changing the enzyme's shape.
At 70 °C, much of the enzyme may have denatured.
Returning to 30 °C restores suitable movement but does not usually restore the denatured active sites.
example.explanation: The recovery test helps distinguish reversible slowing from structural damage.

practice.question: Rates are highest at pH 6 among tests at pH 4, 6 and 8. Can the exact optimum be reported as pH 6.0?
practice.answer: No. pH 6 gave the highest measured rate, but additional values around it are needed to locate the optimum more closely.
practice.explanation: The spacing and uncertainty of observations limit the precision of the conclusion.

commonMistakes: Low temperature usually slows an enzyme; it does not normally denature it.
An observed optimum belongs to the enzyme and conditions tested, not every enzyme.

sections.title: Investigating temperature without changing pH
paragraphs: To isolate temperature, repeat the amylase–starch endpoint experiment at several teacher-approved water-bath temperatures with the same buffer pH. Warm enzyme and substrate separately for the same short equilibration period; the reaction starts when they are combined, not when the tubes first enter the bath.

Measure the actual reaction temperature and keep tubes in the bath during the reaction. Use equal starting concentrations and volumes, the same sampling intervals and fresh enzyme for every run. If the same enzyme portion is successively heated, earlier denaturation changes later runs as well as temperature, confounding the comparison.

Plot relative rate against measured temperature and consider repeat variation. More closely spaced temperatures near a peak help locate the measured optimum. At high temperatures, denaturation can occur during equilibration and measurement, so report both exposure time and temperature.

This endpoint method does not directly distinguish every cause of a slow result. An additional experiment can pre-treat enzyme at two temperatures for equal times and then compare both at one common assay temperature. Persistent loss after heat exposure supports structural damage, whereas recovery after mild cooling supports reversible slowing. This extension needs separate controls and does not replace the basic temperature investigation.

example.question: Mean endpoint times are 120 s at 15 °C, 60 s at 25 °C and 40 s at 35 °C. Compare relative rates at 15 °C and 35 °C.
steps: At 15 °C, relative rate = 1/120 s⁻¹.
At 35 °C, relative rate = 1/40 s⁻¹.
The ratio is (1/40)/(1/120) = 3, so the 35 °C relative rate is three times the 15 °C rate.
These three temperatures do not establish an optimum because no decline has been measured.
example.explanation: The ratio compares rates for an equal endpoint; three rising values cannot locate the peak.

practice.question: Why should each temperature run use a fresh enzyme portion?
practice.answer: Previous high-temperature exposure may have denatured some enzyme, changing the active amount in later tests.
practice.explanation: Fresh portions separate the effect of current test temperature from the history of the sample.

commonMistakes: Do not begin the timer before enzyme and starch have met.
A rising sequence of measured rates does not show the optimum has been reached.

apparatus: Teacher-prepared dilute amylase, starch and one buffer pH
Water baths, thermometer, tubes, timer and sampling pipettes
Dilute iodine and spotting tile
method: Select several safe temperatures and use fresh equal enzyme and substrate portions in each run.
Equilibrate separately for the same fixed period, combine and start timing while maintaining bath temperature.
Test removed samples with iodine at fixed intervals; record endpoint and actual temperature.
Repeat each temperature and include a no-enzyme control; compare relative rates and their variation.
variables: Independent variable: measured reaction temperature. Dependent measure: time to the same endpoint.
Keep buffer pH, initial quantities, pre-incubation period and endpoint procedure constant.
safety: Teacher controls hot-water preparation; prevent scalds and use tube holders when necessary.
Wear eye protection; avoid enzyme dust and contact, and follow buffer and iodine handling instructions.
quality: Keep temperature stable and use the same sampling interval at every condition.
Record endpoint not reached within the chosen duration rather than inventing a completion time.

sections.title: Investigating pH with amylase and starch (Paper 2B)
paragraphs: Amylase breaks starch into smaller sugars. Iodine detects starch, so timed samples can track its disappearance. Put iodine drops on a spotting tile and add a small reaction sample to a fresh drop at each interval. Do not add iodine to the whole reaction tube: it is the indicator used on removed samples.

Change pH using buffer solutions while holding temperature and the starting amounts of starch and enzyme constant. Start timing when enzyme and substrate meet, mix consistently, and sample at fixed intervals. The first sample that no longer turns iodine blue-black is an operational endpoint: starch is below the test's detection threshold, not proven to be absolutely absent.

For the same starting starch amount and endpoint, 1/time is a useful relative rate measure, with units s⁻¹ when time is in seconds. It is not a measured mass of product per second. Record each repeat time, examine the spread and state how the representative rate was calculated.

An interval method only locates the endpoint between two samples. If starch is detected at 50 s but not at 60 s, the threshold was crossed sometime after 50 s and by 60 s. Smaller intervals can improve timing resolution, provided sampling and mixing remain consistent. A result still positive at the stopping time should be recorded as “endpoint not reached”, not as zero activity.
This practical is specified as 2.14B for Paper 2B. The theory of pH effects in 2.13 is shared content and is taught separately from this practical requirement.

example.question: Three runs at one pH reach the endpoint at 50, 60 and 70 s. Calculate the mean time and a relative rate based on that mean.
steps: Relative rate based on mean time = 1 / 60 = 0.0167 s⁻¹ (3 significant figures).
The 20 s range shows variation; it must not be hidden by reporting many decimal places.
The reciprocal of a mean time is not generally the same as the mean of the individual reciprocals.
example.explanation: Name the averaging method explicitly so another person can reproduce the calculation.

practice.question: A pH condition reaches the same endpoint in 30 s instead of 60 s. How do the relative rates compare?
practice.answer: 1/30 is twice 1/60, so the estimated relative rate is doubled.
practice.explanation: For the same change, shorter time means higher rate; it does not mean less reaction.

commonMistakes: Do not put iodine into the reaction mixture being timed.
Do not call 1/time a glucose production rate in grams per second.

apparatus: Teacher-prepared dilute amylase, starch and selected buffer solutions
Dilute iodine, spotting tile, clean pipettes, tubes and timer
Water bath and thermometer
method: Equilibrate separate starch and enzyme portions at a fixed temperature; use identical measured volumes with the selected buffer.
Combine, mix and start the timer together. Test small removed samples with fresh iodine drops every 10 s.
Record the first sample that stays iodine-coloured, and repeat at each pH using fresh solutions.
Include a no-enzyme control and repeat each condition at least three times; plot consistently calculated relative rate against pH.
variables: Independent variable: buffer pH. Dependent measure: time to the defined starch-test endpoint.
Control temperature, starting starch and enzyme amounts, total volume and sampling procedure.
safety: Wear eye protection; use teacher-prepared enzyme solutions and avoid enzyme dust, skin contact and splashes.
Use approved buffers and dilute iodine; do not use saliva or consume materials.
quality: Trial concentrations first so endpoints are measurable; verify final reaction pH where feasible.
Never return iodine-contaminated samples to the tube. Controls check that starch is not disappearing without active enzyme.

sections.title: Diffusion: random motion produces a net movement
paragraphs: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration, caused by their random motion. A concentration gradient is a difference in concentration across a distance. More particles initially leave the more concentrated region than leave the less concentrated region, even though particles move in both directions.

Particles do not sense where they are needed or deliberately travel towards an empty space. Each particle moves randomly. Net movement describes the overall balance across many particles, rather than the direction taken by every particle.

Diffusion can occur through fluids and across a cell membrane if the membrane is permeable to the substance. Oxygen can diffuse into a respiring cell when its concentration is higher outside, while carbon dioxide can diffuse out when its concentration is higher inside. The direction depends on the gradient for that substance, not a universal rule that diffusion always enters cells.

Diffusion does not require energy supplied by respiration. Particles already have kinetic energy. In a closed system at uniform concentration, random motion continues, but there is no net movement down a concentration gradient. Diffusion does not require a membrane; diffusion through agar is a useful non-living model.

example.question: A cell uses oxygen faster than it receives it, so oxygen concentration remains lower inside. Explain the net direction across its oxygen-permeable membrane.
steps: Oxygen moves randomly in both directions.
The higher concentration outside produces a net movement into the cell.
Continual consumption can maintain the gradient; the cell does not pull individual oxygen particles towards itself.
example.explanation: State the substance, compare its concentrations, then explain its net direction.

practice.question: At equal concentrations on both sides of a permeable membrane, do particles stop crossing?
practice.answer: No. Particles continue moving randomly in both directions, with no net movement if other relevant conditions are equal.
practice.explanation: State the substance, compare its concentrations, then explain its net direction.

commonMistakes: Do not say all particles move only from high to low concentration.
Diffusion is not powered by ATP from respiration.

sections.title: Osmosis: water movement across a partially permeable membrane
paragraphs: Osmosis is the net movement of water through a partially permeable membrane from higher water potential to lower water potential. In the simple school model with the same pressure on each side and a solute that cannot cross, this means water moves from the more dilute solution towards the more concentrated solution.

The membrane must allow water through while restricting the relevant solute. Water crosses in both directions; the large arrow in the model represents the net movement. The term osmosis describes water movement, not sugar or salt moving through the membrane.

A plant cell placed in a solution with higher water potential than its contents can take in water. Its vacuole expands and the contents press against the cellulose wall, making the cell turgid. The wall resists further expansion; the pressure that develops reduces the difference in water potential, so inflow need not continue indefinitely.

A plant cell losing water becomes less turgid. In sufficiently concentrated surroundings, its membrane and contents may pull away from the wall: plasmolysis. An animal cell has no supporting cellulose wall and may swell and burst in very dilute surroundings, or shrink after losing water. These outcomes depend on the conditions and the type of cell.

“More concentrated” is a shortcut with assumptions, not the complete definition. Pressure and solute permeability matter. The diagram is an idealised starting comparison with equal pressure, not a measured picture of particles or a claim that every artificial membrane blocks every sugar.

example.question: An ideal membrane passes water but blocks a dissolved solute. At the same initial pressure, side A is more dilute than side B. Predict the initial net movement.
steps: Side A has higher water potential under the stated conditions.
There is a net movement of water A → B through the membrane.
Individual water molecules still cross both ways; the solute is retained in this model.
example.explanation: Name water, give the water-potential direction, and include the membrane.

practice.question: Why does the cellulose wall not replace the membrane in an explanation of osmosis?
practice.answer: The membrane provides selective permeability. The wall provides support and resists swelling; it is not the selectively permeable boundary controlling osmosis.
practice.explanation: Name water, give the water-potential direction, and include the membrane.

commonMistakes: Do not describe the movement of sugar as osmosis.
Dilute-to-concentrated assumes the relevant solute is retained and pressure conditions are comparable.

diagram.alt: Two idealised solution compartments separated by a water-permeable, solute-retaining membrane at equal initial pressure. Water crosses in both directions with an initial net movement from the more dilute left side to the more concentrated right side. The solute stays on its own side. Not to scale.
diagram.caption: An ideal membrane model at equal initial pressure. Small arrows show both-way water movement; the larger arrow shows the initial net direction. Symbols are not measured particle counts.

sections.title: Active transport moves substances against a gradient
paragraphs: Active transport moves substances across a cell membrane against their concentration gradient, from a lower concentration to a higher concentration in this introductory model. Membrane transport proteins are involved, and energy transferred through respiration supplies the process, commonly through ATP.

Root hair cells can take up mineral ions when the ion concentration in the soil solution is lower than in the cell. The uptake helps supply minerals needed by the plant. A concentration comparison and evidence of energy dependence are needed before calling a particular movement active transport: ions can also move down gradients through suitable pathways.

Active transport differs from diffusion in both gradient direction and energy requirement. It differs from osmosis because it transports particular substances using membrane proteins, whereas osmosis is the net movement of water caused by a water-potential difference.

Energy is transferred, not created by mitochondria. ATP can also be supplied through anaerobic processes, so saying that all active transport instantly stops whenever oxygen is absent is too strong. For a specific experiment, the effect depends on the cell, its energy supply and the duration of the treatment.

example.question: The concentration of a mineral ion is 1 arbitrary unit in the soil and 5 units inside a root hair cell. Explain how uptake can still occur.
steps: Uptake from 1 to 5 units goes against this concentration gradient.
Membrane transport proteins use an energy supply to move the ion.
This is consistent with active transport; the numbers alone do not identify every mechanism in a real cell.
example.explanation: Link against-gradient movement to a membrane protein and an energy supply.

practice.question: Is all movement of mineral ions into a root necessarily active transport?
practice.answer: No. The gradient and membrane pathways matter. A concentration gradient into the cell may allow passive movement.
practice.explanation: Link against-gradient movement to a membrane protein and an energy supply.

commonMistakes: Do not claim active transport always moves substances out of cells.
The energy requirement concerns the transport process; diffusion particles still have kinetic energy.

sections.title: Four factors affecting transport rate and surface area per volume
paragraphs: A steeper concentration gradient generally increases the net rate of diffusion when other factors stay the same. Consuming an incoming substance or removing an outgoing substance can help maintain the gradient. As a closed system approaches uniform concentration, net diffusion slows even though particles keep moving.

A shorter diffusion distance allows substances to reach their destination more rapidly. Thin exchange surfaces help. Higher temperature generally increases particles’ kinetic energy and diffusion rate, but heating living tissue too far can damage membranes and proteins; the simple relationship cannot be extended indefinitely.

A larger surface area provides more space for exchange, but a larger organism also contains more material to supply. Surface area to volume ratio compares the available exchange area with the volume requiring supply. It is especially useful when comparing geometrically similar shapes.

For a cube with edge length L, surface area = 6L², volume = L³ and SA/V = 6/L. A cube of edge 1 mm has 6 mm² of surface and 1 mm³ of volume: 6 mm⁻¹. A cube of edge 0.1 mm has 0.06 mm² of surface and 0.001 mm³ of volume: 60 mm⁻¹. The smaller cube has less total surface area but ten times the surface area per unit volume.

This tenfold ratio does not prove that a real cell takes up a substance exactly ten times faster. Permeability, gradients, temperature, shape and diffusion distance also matter. Geometric comparisons support an explanation; they do not replace experimental measurements of rate.

example.question: Compare SA/V for cubes of edge 2 cm and 1 cm, then state a limit of the comparison.
steps: For L = 2 cm: SA = 24 cm², V = 8 cm³ and SA/V = 3 cm⁻¹.
For L = 1 cm: SA = 6 cm², V = 1 cm³ and SA/V = 6 cm⁻¹.
The smaller cube has twice as much surface per unit volume, but an exact uptake-rate ratio needs more evidence.
example.explanation: Separate the measured or calculated ratio from an inference about rate.

practice.question: Why can a small cube have less total surface but a larger SA/V?
practice.answer: Its volume decreases faster than its surface area as edge length decreases: area scales with L² and volume with L³.
practice.explanation: Separate the measured or calculated ratio from an inference about rate.

commonMistakes: Keep length units consistent; SA/V has units of inverse length.
A larger total surface area is not the same as a larger surface area per unit volume.

sections.title: Investigating diffusion into non-living agar
paragraphs: Agar blocks can model how substances penetrate material from its surface. Teacher-prepared alkaline agar containing a suitable indicator changes colour as acid enters and reacts. A visible colour boundary shows where the indicator has responded; it is not a direct image of individual particles.

Compare cubes of different measured sizes after the same immersion time. Measure penetration depth from an outside face to the remaining coloured region. For a cube with a similar depth d on all six faces, the unchanged central edge is L − 2d, provided 0 ≤ d ≤ L/2. The fraction of volume reached is 1 − ((L − 2d)/L)³.

In a purely illustrative calculation, d = 0.1 cm in a cube of edge 1 cm gives a central volume of 0.8³ = 0.512 cm³ and a reached fraction of 48.8%. For a 2 cm cube at the same depth, the central volume is 1.8³ = 5.832 cm³ and the reached fraction is 27.1%. The depth is the same; the fraction reached is different. These are invented teaching inputs, not experimental results.

Agar is not a living cell. It lacks a cell membrane, metabolism and active transport. The colour boundary also depends on reaction and indicator thresholds. Uneven blocks, uneven penetration and reading uncertainty limit the cube calculation. Further practical data and unfamiliar-model comparisons are still needed.

example.question: In the illustrative agar model, a 1 cm cube has a 0.1 cm penetrated layer on every face. Find the percentage of volume reached.
steps: Central edge = 1 − 2(0.1) = 0.8 cm.
Unchanged volume = 0.8³ = 0.512 cm³; original volume = 1 cm³.
Reached percentage = (1 − 0.512) × 100 = 48.8%.
example.explanation: State the model assumptions, calculate the inner core, and interpret the result cautiously.

practice.question: Why is equal penetration depth not evidence that equal proportions of differently sized cubes have been reached?
practice.answer: The remaining core is a different fraction of each cube. Calculate volumes rather than comparing only depth.
practice.explanation: State the model assumptions, calculate the inner core, and interpret the result cautiously.

commonMistakes: Subtract penetration from both sides of an edge.
A colour front reflects a chemical response; it is not a particle speed measurement.

apparatus: Teacher-prepared indicator agar cubes and approved dilute acid
Ruler, timer, forceps, tray and eye protection
method: Measure edge lengths; immerse each cube fully for the same timed interval.
Remove with forceps; a teacher cuts each cube to reveal its core. Measure the colour-boundary depth.
Repeat each size; compare depth and the calculated fraction reached.
variables: Change cube size; keep acid concentration, temperature, immersion time and agar preparation consistent.
safety: Wear eye protection and follow the teacher’s handling instructions for acid and prepared agar.
Keep sharp cutting tools under teacher control; rinse splashes as instructed.
quality: Use enough surrounding solution to avoid substantial depletion; keep all faces exposed.
Record uncertainty and uneven penetration rather than treating the model as exact.

sections.title: Investigating osmosis in living potato tissue
paragraphs: Living potato tissue offers a different model: its cells contain partially permeable membranes. Compare percentage mass changes after immersion in several teacher-prepared sucrose concentrations. Use intact fresh tissue; damaged or dead cells may not behave like healthy cells.

Percentage mass change = ((final mass − initial mass)/initial mass) × 100. Using the initial mass as the denominator lets you compare samples with different starting masses. Blotting consistently before weighing helps avoid counting surface solution as part of the tissue.

For illustrative inputs, a piece changing from 2.00 g to 2.18 g has gained 0.18 g, or +9.0%. Another changing from 2.50 g to 2.20 g has lost 0.30 g, or −12.0%. These arithmetic examples are not obtained laboratory observations.

Plot mean percentage change against sucrose concentration, including repeated measurements and their spread. A crossing of zero can estimate a solution causing no net mass change under the test conditions. Do not automatically call it the exact concentration of every solute inside every potato cell: the tissue contains many cell types and dissolved substances, and water potential is the relevant comparison.

A near-zero change may be within balance uncertainty or result from an insufficient immersion time. Surface liquid, tissue damage, leaching and evaporation can also affect measured mass. Evaluate these possibilities before concluding that water molecules have stopped moving.

example.question: A potato piece changes from 2.50 g to 2.20 g. Calculate its percentage change and interpret the sign.
steps: The tissue lost mass, consistent with net water loss by osmosis if membranes were intact and other mass changes were controlled.
example.explanation: Show a signed change relative to the initial mass, then distinguish observation from interpretation.

practice.question: Why should percentage change use initial rather than final mass?
practice.answer: The initial mass is the comparison baseline. Changing the denominator changes the question being answered.
practice.explanation: Show a signed change relative to the initial mass, then distinguish observation from interpretation.

commonMistakes: Do not discard a negative sign for mass loss.
Zero net mass change does not mean water molecules stop moving.

apparatus: Fresh equal-dimension potato pieces, labelled sucrose solutions and water
Balance, paper towel, forceps, containers and timer
method: Prepare fresh pieces with matching dimensions; blot consistently and record each starting mass.
Immerse in equal volumes of the labelled solutions for a fixed time at the same temperature.
Remove, blot in the same way and weigh. Repeat using fresh pieces; calculate percentage changes.
variables: Change sucrose concentration; measure percentage mass change.
Keep tissue source, dimensions, solution volume, temperature, time and blotting procedure consistent.
safety: A teacher prepares pieces with sharp tools. Do not eat the tissue or drink laboratory solutions.
quality: Include a water condition and several concentrations; record repeats and balance resolution.
Investigate unusual values instead of discarding them solely because they disagree with the expected trend.

sections.title: Testing a non-living membrane model and its limits
paragraphs: A teacher-prepared dialysis bag containing starch and glucose can be immersed in water. The selected tubing allows glucose to pass but retains starch over the test period. Testing separate outside samples before and after immersion can provide evidence that some substances cross the membrane and others do not.

Rinse the outside before immersion so leaked filling solution does not produce a false initial positive result. Use controls for the reducing-sugar and starch tests. For this prepared mixture, a new positive reducing-sugar result outside is consistent with glucose crossing down its gradient. Benedict’s reagent detects reducing sugars generally; it is not a glucose-specific identification test.

This is a non-living model of selective permeability and diffusion. It does not contain living intestinal cells, enzymes or membrane transport proteins, and it cannot demonstrate active transport. The artificial tubing’s permeability must be checked for the actual molecules and conditions used.

Do not assume all sugars are excluded just because starch is retained. Some tubing also passes sucrose. A reliable osmosis demonstration needs a membrane that retains the selected solute during the observation; otherwise solute diffusion changes the gradient. Bag mass changes alone cannot identify which substances crossed.

example.question: The outside water is initially negative for reducing sugar and later positive, while the starch test stays negative. What conclusion is supported for a known glucose-and-starch filling mixture?
steps: The result is consistent with glucose reaching the outside through the selected membrane.
No starch was detected outside by the test used; this does not establish the membrane blocks every solute.
Leaks, contaminated outside surfaces and test controls must be considered.
example.explanation: Use the controls and known mixture to draw a bounded conclusion, then state what the model omits.

practice.question: Does this dialysis model prove intestinal absorption uses only diffusion?
practice.answer: No. It is an artificial non-living membrane. A real gut contains living cells and transport mechanisms that the model lacks.
practice.explanation: Use the controls and known mixture to draw a bounded conclusion, then state what the model omits.

commonMistakes: Starch retention does not imply sucrose retention.
A reducing-sugar test is not specific to glucose in an unknown sample.

apparatus: Teacher-prepared hydrated dialysis bags with known glucose-and-starch mixture
Water, clean sampling pipettes, iodine and Benedict’s test reagents
Teacher-controlled water bath, test tubes, timer and eye protection
method: Rinse the filled bag’s outside, seal and check for leaks; immerse in fresh water.
Test separate outside samples at the start and after the same timed interval, keeping test reagents out of the bath.
Include a water blank, known test-positive controls and a sealed water-filled bag control; repeat.
variables: Measure outside test results over a controlled interval.
Keep membrane grade and exposed area, solution volumes, filling concentrations and temperature consistent.
safety: Wear eye protection; a teacher manages the hot bath and reagent handling.
Use laboratory-prepared samples and do not consume them.
quality: Verify the chosen tubing’s glucose/starch permeability rather than assuming it from the brand name.
A positive outside test may reflect a leak or contamination; controls and inspection are needed.

sections.title: Photosynthesis transfers light energy into organic molecules
paragraphs: Photosynthesis uses light energy to make organic molecules from carbon dioxide and water. Chlorophyll in chloroplasts absorbs light. The energy is transferred into chemical energy associated with the products; the plant does not create energy or obtain all its food ready-made from the soil.

The school word equation is carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, with light and chlorophyll stated as conditions. The balanced net symbol equation is 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. Both sides contain six C, twelve H and eighteen O atoms. Light supplies energy rather than being an extra material atom in the equation.

Glucose can be used in respiration, converted into starch for storage and used to make cellulose and other substances. Plants also need mineral ions to make molecules such as proteins. Photosynthesis supports plant biomass and supplies organic material to many food chains.

Plants respire in light and darkness. Photosynthesis requires suitable light, but respiration is not switched off when photosynthesis occurs. The net gas exchange observed around a plant reflects both processes, not photosynthesis alone.

example.question: Check the atom balance in 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ and name the energy transfer.
steps: Absorbed light energy is transferred into chemical energy in organic products.
example.explanation: Keep matter accounting, energy transfer and the pigment’s role separate.

practice.question: Is chlorophyll a reactant consumed in the word equation?
practice.answer: No. It absorbs light and is a condition for photosynthesis in this model, not a stoichiometric reactant in the net equation.
practice.explanation: Keep matter accounting, energy transfer and the pigment’s role separate.

commonMistakes: Do not say plants get their glucose food from the soil.
Plants also respire during daylight.

sections.title: Light, carbon dioxide and temperature can limit the rate
paragraphs: A limiting factor is a condition preventing the rate from rising under the current circumstances. At low light intensity, increasing light can increase photosynthesis because more energy is available. Eventually another factor may limit the process, so the graph need not continue rising at the same rate.

Increasing carbon dioxide availability can increase the rate when carbon dioxide supply is limiting and other requirements are adequate. If light is very low, adding carbon dioxide may have little effect. A plateau alone does not identify which other factor is limiting without additional tests.

Photosynthesis includes enzyme-controlled reactions. Warming within a suitable range can increase reaction rate, but excessive heat can damage proteins and other cell processes, decreasing the rate. An observed optimum depends on the plant and conditions; there is no single optimum temperature for every plant.

Changing a lamp’s distance may change temperature as well as light intensity. Measure or control these separately. A valid explanation connects a particular condition to the process, rather than asserting that everything warmer or brighter always makes photosynthesis faster.

example.question: A plant’s measured gas release rises with light, then levels off. What can you infer, and what remains uncertain?
steps: Light was limiting over the increasing part, assuming other conditions stayed comparable.
At the plateau, increasing light alone no longer increased the measured release.
Test other factors and measurement limits before naming carbon dioxide as the definite new limiter.
example.explanation: Use the pattern to identify a supported limitation and state what further evidence is needed.

practice.question: Would carbon dioxide necessarily increase the rate in almost complete darkness?
practice.answer: No. Light availability can remain limiting even after more carbon dioxide is supplied.
practice.explanation: Use the pattern to identify a supported limitation and state what further evidence is needed.

commonMistakes: A plateau does not name its cause without more evidence.

sections.title: Connect a typical leaf’s structure to its functions
paragraphs: A typical broad leaf presents a large area to light and is thin, giving short distances for light penetration and gas diffusion. A transparent upper epidermis lets light reach the photosynthetic tissues. A waxy cuticle helps limit water loss; it is not the main gas-exchange opening.

Palisade mesophyll cells lie near the upper surface in this typical leaf and contain many chloroplasts, placing light-absorbing pigment near incoming light. Spongy mesophyll has air spaces connecting cells to stomata, providing internal surfaces for diffusion. Some spongy cells also contain chloroplasts.

Stomata are pores controlled by guard cells. Carbon dioxide can diffuse into the leaf through these pores and oxygen can diffuse out when its internal concentration is higher. Guard-cell control also affects water-vapour loss, so gas exchange and water conservation must be balanced.

Veins contain xylem delivering water and mineral ions, and phloem transporting organic solutes such as sucrose. A feature-based explanation links structure to light capture, carbon dioxide supply, water supply or product transport. This is a typical leaf model; specialised leaves and stomatal distributions vary.

example.question: Explain how air spaces in spongy mesophyll help photosynthesis.
steps: They connect the stomatal openings with internal leaf surfaces.
Carbon dioxide can diffuse through the spaces towards photosynthetic cells.
Short diffusion paths help supply the carbon dioxide used in photosynthesis.
example.explanation: Name a structure and connect its particular feature to a useful process.

practice.question: Why is “the leaf is thin” incomplete when asked to explain an adaptation?
practice.answer: It needs a functional link, such as short gas-diffusion distance or light reaching photosynthetic cells.
practice.explanation: Name a structure and connect its particular feature to a useful process.

commonMistakes: Do not confuse xylem water delivery with phloem sugar transport.

sections.title: Magnesium and nitrate ions support growth
paragraphs: Plants need mineral ions as well as the materials and energy required for photosynthesis. Roots absorb dissolved ions from the surroundings. Mineral nutrition supplies elements for plant molecules; it does not replace photosynthesis as the source of newly made carbohydrates.

Magnesium is part of chlorophyll, so insufficient magnesium can reduce chlorophyll formation and cause chlorosis, a loss of green colour. Nitrate supplies nitrogen for amino acids, which are joined to make proteins used in growth and many cell processes.

Nitrate deficiency can limit growth because amino-acid and protein production is restricted. Symptoms are clues rather than an automatic diagnosis: other deficiencies, disease and environmental stresses can produce similar changes. Compare with an appropriate complete-nutrient control before assigning a cause.
Magnesium ions are not molecules of chlorophyll, and nitrate ions are not ready-made amino acids. The plant incorporates their elements into more complex molecules through its chemical processes.

example.question: Connect magnesium and nitrate deficiencies to the molecules affected.
steps: Magnesium shortage can impair chlorophyll production and light capture.
Nitrate shortage restricts the nitrogen supply for amino acids and proteins.
A symptom alone does not establish the deficient ion without a controlled comparison.
example.explanation: Connect each ion to its specific molecular role and then to growth or photosynthesis.

practice.question: Does adding nitrate give a plant pre-made protein?
practice.answer: No. Nitrate supplies nitrogen that the plant can use to make amino acids and then proteins.
practice.explanation: Connect each ion to its specific molecular role and then to growth or photosynthesis.

commonMistakes: Mineral ions supply elements; they are not the whole organic molecules.

sections.title: Investigating oxygen release from a water plant
paragraphs: A living water plant in suitable light can release gas containing oxygen during photosynthesis. A teacher-prepared collection setup can collect the gas for an approved oxygen test. Oxygen relights a glowing splint; seeing bubbles alone does not establish their composition.

To compare release rates, collect volume during a fixed interval and divide by time. Counting bubbles is a rougher proxy because bubble sizes vary. Dissolved gas, leaks and the plant’s own respiration affect the measured release; it is not automatically the gross photosynthesis rate.

With illustrative inputs only, 1.8 cm³ collected over 3.0 minutes gives 0.60 cm³ min⁻¹. A second condition giving 3.0 cm³ over the same interval gives 1.0 cm³ min⁻¹. The ratio is 5/3, about 1.67; this is an arithmetic example, not a measured response to any specific lamp.

When varying light, keep water temperature and carbon dioxide availability comparable, allow adjustment after changes and repeat. Use a consistent healthy plant amount and collection geometry. A no-plant setup can check background effects such as trapped air.

example.question: Calculate gas release rate for 1.8 cm³ in 3.0 minutes and state one limit of using it as a photosynthesis measure.
steps: Rate=1.8/3.0=0.60 cm³ min⁻¹.
This measures collected gas, not every molecule produced.
Gas dissolution, collection losses and respiration affect the interpretation.
example.explanation: Calculate the stated measured rate and distinguish it from the biological rate inferred.

practice.question: Why is bubble count weaker than a volume measurement?
practice.answer: Bubbles can have different sizes, so equal counts need not mean equal gas volumes.
practice.explanation: Calculate the stated measured rate and distinguish it from the biological rate inferred.

commonMistakes: Bubbles are evidence of gas release, not proof of pure oxygen.

apparatus: Healthy teacher-selected water plant and a suitable gas collection setup
Light source, thermometer, timer and approved carbon dioxide supply
Teacher-controlled oxygen test equipment
method: Assemble the approved setup without trapped air and record initial conditions.
Allow the plant to adjust; collect gas over a fixed timed interval.
The teacher tests a separate collected sample for oxygen; repeat volume/time readings.
If varying light, keep water temperature and carbon dioxide supply controlled.
variables: Change only the intended light condition; measure collected gas volume per unit time.
Keep plant amount, collection arrangement, temperature and solution preparation comparable.
safety: Keep electrical equipment away from splashed water; the teacher controls gas tests and any hot or sharp tools.
quality: Check leaks and use a no-plant control; unequal bubble size limits bubble counting.
Record actual observations and repeat spread; expected oxygen release is not an obtained result.

sections.title: Use a starch test after checking the starting condition
paragraphs: A leaf starch test detects starch present at the time of testing. Iodine gives a blue-black result where sufficient starch is present. It does not directly measure the momentary photosynthesis rate or test glucose specifically.

For a requirement experiment, first reduce pre-existing starch by keeping a healthy plant in darkness for a suitable teacher-planned period, commonly a day or two. Check a sample leaf before the treatment: time in darkness alone is not proof that every leaf has become starch-free. In darkness, light-driven photosynthesis stops; stored starch can be broken down to sugars used in respiration or moved to other parts of the plant.

The teacher-supervised test kills the sampled leaf in hot water, removes chlorophyll with ethanol in a safe hot-water bath, then rinses/softens the leaf before iodine is applied on a light background. Removing pigment makes the colour response easier to distinguish.

Ethanol is highly flammable. Use the approved bath method with all naked flames absent while ethanol is handled; do not heat ethanol directly over a burner. A known starch-positive material and a suitable blank help check the test reagent and colour interpretation.

example.question: Why check an initial leaf after the planned destarching period?
steps: A negative initial starch test supports the intended starting condition.
Otherwise a later positive result could reflect starch already present before the treatment.
The control strengthens the interpretation without measuring the precise photosynthesis rate.
example.explanation: Check the starting starch and the test system before attributing a later result to the treatment.

practice.question: Does a blue-black result alone prove that starch was made during the most recent light exposure?
practice.answer: No. Pre-existing starch must be considered, which is why the starting condition is checked.
practice.explanation: Check the starting starch and the test system before attributing a later result to the treatment.

commonMistakes: A starch test is not a glucose-specific test or a direct instantaneous rate measure.

apparatus: Healthy starting-control and treated leaves
Teacher-managed hot water and an ethanol water-bath setup with no naked flames
Forceps, white tile and dilute iodine
method: Check starting starch on a sample leaf before the planned light or requirement treatment.
After treatment, the teacher uses hot water then a safe ethanol bath to remove pigment.
Rinse and soften the leaf, lay it on a pale background and apply iodine.
Compare mapped regions and test controls using the same procedure.
variables: Measure detectable starch colour after the chosen treatment.
Keep test preparation, iodine application and reading conditions consistent.
safety: Ethanol is flammable: no naked flames while it is used and no direct flame heating.
The teacher manages hot apparatus and reagents; wear eye protection and use forceps.
quality: Use a known starch-positive comparison and blank to check the reagent.
A starch-negative starting sample improves interpretation but is not a guarantee for every leaf.

sections.title: Compare illuminated and green regions of a leaf
paragraphs: To investigate light, use a plant with its starting starch checked, shield a selected leaf region with an opaque cover, and expose the plant to suitable light. Mark covered and exposed areas before taking the leaf for the same starch-test procedure.

The expected controlled comparison is starch in exposed green tissue and little or no detectable starch in the shaded region. It supports the need for light in starch accumulation during the trial. A mask can also alter the leaf’s local conditions, so check plant health and interpret the comparison with those limitations.

To investigate chlorophyll, use a variegated leaf and record its green and non-green regions before pigment is removed. After an appropriate light period, compare the starch response with the original pattern. The usual result is strongest starch response in green illuminated tissue.

Use healthy controls, repeat with further leaves and keep the light period and other conditions comparable. This is evidence supporting chlorophyll’s role, not proof that every possible pale region is identical except for one molecule. No leaf colour map or starch outcome has been obtained in this project.

example.question: Why draw the green-region pattern of a variegated leaf before the starch test?
steps: The ethanol step removes the pigment used to locate the original green areas.
The map allows starch-test regions to be compared with the earlier chlorophyll pattern.
Without that record, assigning the final regions can be unreliable.
example.explanation: Match each tested region to its original condition and use a positive comparison.

practice.question: Why keep some green tissue exposed when testing whether light is required?
practice.answer: It provides a positive comparison under the same general conditions, helping distinguish treatment effects from a failed trial.
practice.explanation: Match each tested region to its original condition and use a positive comparison.

commonMistakes: Record the original colour pattern before removing pigment.

sections.title: Compare carbon dioxide supply with a matched control
paragraphs: A teacher-prepared closed-container comparison can test carbon dioxide availability. Begin with healthy plants whose starting starch is checked. One container includes an approved carbon dioxide absorber isolated from the plant; a matched control allows carbon dioxide to remain available.

Expose both to similar suitable light for the same period, then use the same leaf starch test. A positive control and a negative or weaker absorber-treatment response support the need for carbon dioxide for new starch accumulation under the tested conditions.

The absorber must not contact the plant. Containers, initial plant size and condition, watering, temperature and light should match. An absorber can also alter humidity, and container leaks can admit carbon dioxide, so these are evaluation issues rather than hidden assumptions that the setups are perfectly identical.

The teacher prepares and handles the corrosive absorber, such as approved potassium hydroxide solution, through the school’s risk controls. This is a study description of the comparison. A failed positive control, unhealthy leaves or an unverified starting starch condition prevents a strong conclusion.

example.question: Both absorber and control leaves give negative starch tests. Can the trial establish a carbon dioxide requirement?
steps: The intended positive control failed.
Light, plant condition, starting treatment or the test itself may have prevented a detectable result.
Repeat with verified controls before attributing the difference to carbon dioxide supply.
example.explanation: Use a working control and rule out damaging or mismatched conditions before attributing a result to carbon dioxide.

practice.question: Why must the absorber be separated from the leaf?
practice.answer: Direct chemical contact could damage tissue and create a different cause for a negative starch result.
practice.explanation: Use a working control and rule out damaging or mismatched conditions before attributing a result to carbon dioxide.

commonMistakes: A negative treatment without a working positive control is weak evidence.
